extracted.intended_audience: students and general readers interested in foundations and philosophy of mathematics (advanced undergraduates, graduate students, mathematicians, philosophers)
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts and summarizes foundational criteria and conceptual standards used in mathematics for defining existence, validating proofs, handling infinity, and axiomatizing randomness (the fair coin). Targets conceptual evaluation rather than formal problem-solving.

rubrics_metrics.name: Filter in a set (definition/criteria)
rubrics_metrics.description: Let X be a set and F a family of non-empty subsets of X such that (1) if two sets A and B belong to F, then so does their intersection; (2) if A belongs to F and A is a subset of B (subset of X), then B belongs to F. Such a family F is called a filter in X.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: the Fréchet filter on positive integers (cofinite sets) — subsets omitting only finitely many elements. Anti-pattern: the set of odd numbers is not in the Fréchet filter because it omits infinitely many even numbers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ultrafilter existence (maximal filter)
rubrics_metrics.description: A maximal filter V containing a given filter F is a filter in X such that adding any subset of X not already in V causes V to cease to be a filter. Such an object is called an ultrafilter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Existence can be shown using the principle that every set can be well-ordered (uses Choice-like principles). Particularization: there is a Fréchet ultrafilter. Note: understanding what an ultrafilter contains is nontrivial and central to set theory/logic investigations; existence depends on ambient axioms (see Axiom of Choice).

rubrics_metrics.name: Existence of mathematical objects is context-dependent
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no single notion of existence for mathematical objects; existence is intimately related to setting, demands, and function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: sqrt(2) does not exist as an integer or fraction but 'exists' within the real numbers; a real number may 'exist' as a construction rule or program even if not a completed decimal; the Fréchet ultrafilter exists within mathematics that accepts the Axiom of Choice. Implication: acceptance of existence claims depends on the chosen axioms and the intended mathematical milieu.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof as the defining feature and validation mechanism
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematics is characterized by proof; proof functions as validation and certification of mathematical statements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proofs refer backwards to prior propositions and ultimately stop at axioms and definitions. Proofs serve to persuade, certify truth 'beyond the shadow of a doubt', and place statements within a validated structure. Historical example: Euclid's Pythagorean proof and the chain of references Hobbes experienced.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formal characteristics of mathematical proof
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematical proofs use a formal, severely restricted language, high abstraction, and often rely on diagrams/figures as essential adjuncts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Figures may be necessary to follow Euclidean-style arguments; proofs use construction lines that reorganize figures into subfigures. The language differs from narrative or everyday language and is refined to serve precise goals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purposes/functions of proof beyond mere correctness
rubrics_metrics.description: Proof serves multiple simultaneous purposes: revalidation under scrutiny, error correction, increased understanding, suggestion of new mathematics, training for creation of new results, conferment of respectability and authority, and ritual celebration of reason.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: repeated reproving of classical theorems clarifies ambiguities and reveals deeper structure; proofs 'vitalize' static assertions and can be a source of mathematical power and new directions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heuristic/creative aspect of finding proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no guaranteed method to find proofs; constructing them often requires ingenuity and skill (e.g., choosing appropriate construction lines in geometry).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Finding such construction or auxiliary lines can be accidental or fortuitous and improves with experience. Anti-pattern: expecting a mechanical recipe guaranteeing a proof for arbitrary problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Axioms may omit intuitive facts (need for additional axioms)
rubrics_metrics.description: Intuitive facts about mathematical objects may not be derivable from a given axiom set and sometimes must be added as axioms (e.g., Pasch's axiom for betweenness on lines).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical note: Pasch noticed an omission in Euclid in 1882; some Euclidean theorems require Pasch's axiom. Similarly, Skolem showed nonstandard models of arithmetic satisfy the axioms yet differ from intended natural numbers, indicating axioms can be incomplete with respect to intuition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition/criterion for an infinite set
rubrics_metrics.description: An infinite set is one which can be put into one-to-one correspondence with a proper subset of itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This distinguishes infinite arithmetic from finite; examples and paradoxes (Galileo) illustrate how infinite behavior differs from finite intuition. Implication: operations valid for finite numbers may be invalid when naively applied to infinite cardinals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Axiom of Infinity (formal requirement)
rubrics_metrics.description: In axiomatic set theory: 'An inductive (i.e., infinite) set exists.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This axiom institutionalizes the mathematical request to accept infinite sets. Comparison/contrast with theological/philosophical axioms is drawn in text to illuminate self-evidence questions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cantorian cardinal arithmetic cautions
rubrics_metrics.description: Infinite cardinals obey arithmetic laws different from finite ones (e.g., N0 + 1 = N0, N0 + N0 = N0), so one must not manipulate them as if finite.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-pattern: subtracting N0 from both sides of an equation as if finite leads to paradoxes. Philosophical question: how 'infinite' is an object that is encapsulated algorithmically?

rubrics_metrics.name: Regularization methods for paradoxes involving infinity
rubrics_metrics.description: Paradoxes arising from infinite processes are handled by imposing qualifications and using refined theories: limits, absolute convergence, uniform convergence, compactness, nonstandard analysis, operational calculi, and distribution theory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Berkeley's infinitesimals were handled by limiting-process reformulations and later by nonstandard analysis; Dirac's delta is addressed by Schwartz distributions or other operational calculi. Practical rule: restrict to contexts (e.g., absolute convergence) where manipulations are justified.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuum Hypothesis (CH) undecidability under usual axioms
rubrics_metrics.description: Within the Zermelo-Fraenkel (and related) axiomatic systems, neither the continuum hypothesis nor its negation can be proved (Gödel and Cohen).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CH is also undecidable in an intuitive sense—no compelling intuition currently selects it or its negation—so one may add CH or its negation as an extra axiom to obtain different 'versions' of the continuum/straight line.

rubrics_metrics.name: Frequency/probability characterization of a fair coin
rubrics_metrics.description: For a fair coin tossed n times producing counts H(n) and T(n), H(n)+T(n)=n and lim_{n->∞} H(n)/n = 1/2, lim_{n->∞} T(n)/n = 1/2; these limits define P(H)=1/2, P(T)=1/2.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The frequency view does not demand exact halves for finite n; probabilities are limits. This is a foundation for frequency probability and leads to further probabilistic assumptions under mixing/combining.

rubrics_metrics.name: Insensitivity to place selection (subsequence invariance for fair coin)
rubrics_metrics.description: The limiting frequencies (1/2 each) persist even when observing subsequences chosen by many selection rules (e.g., odd-indexed tosses, squares-indexed tosses, or those selected after certain prior histories).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implication: place selection according to policies depending on prior history does not yield biased subsequence frequencies for an ideal fair coin. This supports the notion that 'long-run' balance is robust under many selection schemes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle of impotence (no successful gambling system)
rubrics_metrics.description: One cannot devise a successful gambling system to exploit a fair coin—i.e., there is no place-selection-based betting method that yields a consistent advantage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a physicists' phrasing for the robustness of fairness; historically perceived early and foundational for probability theory. Anti-pattern: attempts to exploit runs or place-selection to gain an edge (gambler's fallacy).

rubrics_metrics.name: Question of applicability: mapping abstract models to real-world coins
rubrics_metrics.description: The abstract fair coin and idealized randomness axioms are idealized constructs; one must question how the mathematical theory relates to the behavior of real-world coins.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is an epistemic criterion: theory must be checked against empirical behavior and physical considerations; the text raises but does not resolve this philosophical/empirical gap.
